questions.q: Etowah, a Mississippian town with tall flat-topped mounds and finely worked copper plates, stands beside a river near Cartersville in which present-day state?
questions.explain: Etowah was occupied from about 1000 to 1550; its largest mound rises more than 60 feet above the Etowah River valley.

questions.q: At Ocmulgee near Macon, Georgia, archaeologists uncovered the clay floor of a round council building with a raised bench and a bird-shaped platform. What kind of structure was it?
questions.explain: The Ocmulgee earth lodge, dated to about 1015, was rebuilt by the Park Service in the 1930s over its original floor.

questions.q: Archaeologists group the shared Mississippian images found on copper plates and shell gorgets from Spiro to Etowah, such as falcon-winged dancers and forked eyes, under what name?
questions.explain: The Southeastern Ceremonial Complex, also called the Mississippian Ideological Interaction Sphere, reflects religious ideas shared across many chiefdoms.

questions.q: Mississippian peoples, including those at Cahokia, played chunkey. What did players do in this game?
options: Kicked a rubber ball through a stone ring
Hit a deerskin ball over a net of cords
Threw spears at a rolling stone disk
questions.explain: Players hurled poles where they thought the rolling disk would stop; polished chunkey stones are found at many Mississippian sites.

questions.q: Old Oraibi, a Hopi village on Third Mesa that has been lived in since about the 1100s, is in which present-day state?
questions.explain: Oraibi is often cited as one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the United States.

questions.q: Taos Pueblo, a multistory adobe town lived in for about a thousand years, sits at the foot of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in which present-day state?
questions.explain: Taos Pueblo was named a National Historic Landmark in 1960 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992.

questions.q: Hopi farmers on the dry mesas of northern Arizona raised corn with very little rain. Which method helped them do it?
options: Flooding fields from stone-lined mountain reservoirs
Building raised garden beds in shallow lakes
Planting seeds deep in sandy soil to reach moisture
Clearing new forest plots by burning each spring
questions.explain: Hopi dry farming placed seeds as much as a foot deep, in fields sited where runoff and sand held water.

questions.q: Long before Spaniards arrived, Hopi and other Pueblo weavers made kilts, sashes and blankets from which fiber that they grew themselves?
questions.explain: Pueblo peoples grew a drought-tolerant cotton; among the Hopi, men traditionally did the weaving.

questions.q: Mimbres potters of southwestern New Mexico, working from about 1000 to 1130, are best known for what?
options: Black-on-white bowls painted with animals and people
Glazed blue-and-white tiles for temple walls
Giant carved stone heads of their rulers
Copper bells cast in clay molds for trade
questions.explain: Many Mimbres bowls were buried with the dead, often with a small hole punched through the bottom.

questions.q: Tlingit and other northern Northwest Coast weavers made Chilkat robes, worn at ceremonies, from what materials?
options: Mountain goat wool and cedar bark
questions.explain: A single Chilkat robe, woven in bold formline designs, could take a weaver a year or more to finish.

questions.q: Northwest Coast peoples traded oil rendered from the eulachon along inland routes called grease trails. What is a eulachon?
options: A large sea mammal of the northern Pacific
A shellfish gathered from tidal flats
A small, oily fish of the smelt family
A cedar tree whose sap was boiled down
questions.explain: Eulachon are so oily that a dried one can be lit like a candle, which is why they are also called candlefish.

questions.q: The Makah, at the northwestern tip of present-day Washington State, were known for which ocean skill?
options: Diving for pearls in warm lagoons
Farming kelp in walled sea pens
Boiling seawater to make salt cakes
questions.explain: Makah whaling was central to their culture; their 1855 Treaty of Neah Bay expressly protected the right to hunt whales.

questions.q: Among many Northwest Coast peoples before European contact, how did a person usually become enslaved?
options: By being captured in a raid on another group
By being sentenced for debt by a tribal court
By being sold by a parent during a famine year
By losing a wager at a potlatch feast
questions.explain: Captives taken in raids, and their descendants, formed a slave class owned by high-ranking households.

questions.q: Why did Iroquoian farming towns in the Northeast usually move to a new site every couple of decades?
options: Spanish slave raiders had found them
Nearby soil and firewood were worn out
Spring floods washed away their fields
Their law forbade burying the dead twice
questions.explain: Nearby fields lost fertility and the forest near the palisade was cut over, the standard explanation for why the whole town relocated a few miles away.

questions.q: Southeastern peoples brewed the ceremonial 'black drink,' a strong caffeinated tea taken before councils, from the leaves of which plant?
questions.explain: Yaupon is the most caffeine-rich plant native to North America; its scientific name, Ilex vomitoria, recalls purging rituals.

questions.q: The Green Corn Ceremony, or Busk, held by the Muscogee (Creek) and other Southeastern peoples, marked what?
options: The first snowfall and the start of winter hunts
A victory over enemies in a recent war
The return of migrating bison to the river
Renewal and forgiveness as the new corn ripened
questions.explain: Towns rekindled sacred fires, cleaned houses and forgave many offenses before the new corn could be eaten.

questions.q: In 1540 Hernando de Soto's expedition was received by a woman ruler, known to the Spanish as the Lady of Cofitachequi, in what is now which state?
questions.explain: The Lady gave the Spaniards pearls, but de Soto took her captive; she later escaped from the expedition.

questions.q: Among the Taino of the Caribbean, what was a cacique?
options: A carved stone image of a spirit
A chief who ruled a village or a larger district
A field of mounded earth for cassava
A plaza where ball games were played
questions.explain: Spaniards carried the Taino word cacique across their empire, using it for Native leaders from Mexico to Peru.

questions.q: Taino farmers grew cassava in mounded fields called conucos. Before grating bitter cassava roots into bread flour, what did they have to remove?
questions.explain: Bitter cassava contains cyanide compounds, so the grated pulp was squeezed dry before baking flat cassava bread.

questions.q: The Viceroyalty of Peru, created by Spain in 1542, was governed from which city founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535?
questions.explain: Lima, the City of Kings, was the seat of Spanish rule over most of South America for nearly three centuries.

questions.q: Spain's treasure fleets from Veracruz and the Isthmus of Panama gathered at which Caribbean port before sailing home together under naval escort?
questions.explain: Under the fleet system set up in the 1560s, the convoys met at Havana and then caught the Gulf Stream past Florida.

questions.q: Where was the first printing press in the Americas set up, in 1539?
questions.explain: Juan Pablos ran the press for the Seville printer Juan Cromberger; its early books were mostly religious works for missionaries.

questions.q: Spaniards built Mexico City's cathedral beside the ruined sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan. What was its great pyramid, crowned by twin shrines, called?
questions.explain: Its twin shrines honored Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc; excavation of its ruins began in earnest in 1978.

questions.q: Which mid-Atlantic island chain, roughly 850 miles west of Portugal, did the Portuguese begin settling in the 1430s?
questions.explain: The Azores, Madeira and Cape Verde became stepping stones for Portuguese voyages and testing grounds for colonization.

questions.q: By about 1500, which Portuguese-settled Atlantic island had become one of Europe's leading sources of sugar?
questions.explain: Madeira's sugar mills, worked partly by enslaved people, offered an early model of the plantation system later carried to Brazil.

questions.q: In 1492, the same year as Columbus's first voyage, Ferdinand and Isabella ordered which group to convert to Christianity or leave Spain?
questions.explain: The Alhambra Decree forced tens of thousands into exile; Muslims in Castile faced a similar order in 1502.

questions.q: The 1469 marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand joined which two Iberian kingdoms, laying the base for a united Spain?
questions.explain: Each kingdom kept its own laws, but together the Catholic Monarchs finished the Reconquista and backed Columbus.

questions.q: Juan de la Cosa, a mapmaker who sailed with Columbus, drew a world map in 1500 that is notable as what?
options: The first map to use the name America
The first map drawn with the Mercator projection
The first printed atlas of the known world
The oldest surviving European map to show the Americas
questions.explain: His manuscript chart, now in Madrid, shows Caribbean islands and coastline as a green landmass west of the Atlantic.

questions.q: A 1513 world map that survives in part, showing the Atlantic coasts of South America and Africa and said to draw on a Columbus chart, was made by an admiral of which empire?
questions.explain: Piri Reis drew the map on gazelle-skin parchment; it was rediscovered in Istanbul's Topkapi Palace in 1929.

questions.q: Martin Behaim's globe, made in Nuremberg in 1492 and the oldest surviving globe of the earth, leaves out which landmass?
questions.explain: Finished just before news of Columbus reached Europe, it shows open ocean between Europe and Asia.

questions.q: Abraham Ortelius's Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, published in Antwerp in 1570, is usually regarded as what?
options: The first globe to show the Pacific
The first sea chart of Newfoundland
The first map to show Cuba as an island
questions.explain: It gathered uniform maps of the world into one bound book and went through dozens of editions.

questions.q: Juan Ponce de Leon named Florida in 1513 partly because he arrived near which Christian holiday season?
questions.explain: The Spanish called Easter Pascua Florida, the flowery feast, and the coast was also green with plants.

questions.q: Where did the name California come from?
options: An island of women warriors in a Spanish romance novel
A Chumash word for the land beyond the sea
The name of Hernan Cortes's flagship
A saint honored on the day Cabrillo landed
questions.explain: Garci Rodriguez de Montalvo's novel Las Sergas de Esplandian, printed about 1510, described an island named California.

questions.q: The first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas broke out in 1518-1519 on which island before reaching Mexico?
questions.explain: Smallpox ravaged the remaining Taino and soon spread to the mainland, where it struck Tenochtitlan in 1520.

questions.q: In 1545 and again in 1576, devastating epidemics killed a large share of the Native people of New Spain. By what name, from the Aztec word for pestilence, are they known?
questions.explain: The cause of the cocoliztli epidemics is still debated; they were among the deadliest disease outbreaks in Mexico's history.

questions.q: Which animals did Andean peoples domesticate to carry loads and supply wool long before Europeans arrived?
questions.explain: Llama caravans carried goods along Inca roads, while alpaca fleece made fine cloth.

questions.q: High in the Andes, people preserved potatoes as chuno, which could keep for years. How did they make it?
options: By freezing them at night and drying them in the sun
By salting them in sealed clay jars
By smoking them over slow fires of dung
By burying them in hot desert sand
questions.explain: Repeated frosts, sun and trampling squeezed out the water, leaving light potatoes that fed armies and storehouses.

questions.q: Machu Picchu, high in the Peruvian Andes, is generally thought to have been built as an estate for which Inca ruler?
questions.explain: Built in the mid-1400s, the site escaped Spanish notice and became internationally famous after Hiram Bingham's 1911 visit.

questions.q: The Inca road system, which ran thousands of miles along the Andes and down the Pacific coast, is known by what Quechua name?
questions.explain: Relay runners called chasquis carried messages and quipus along the roads, which included rope suspension bridges.

questions.q: The Inca called their empire Tawantinsuyu. What does the name mean?
questions.explain: The empire was divided into four quarters, or suyus, which met at the capital, Cuzco.

questions.q: In 1516 the friar Tomas de Berlanga is credited with bringing which crop from the Canary Islands to Hispaniola?
questions.explain: Bananas and plantains, originally from Southeast Asia, spread quickly through tropical America after 1516.

questions.q: What was the title of the Mexica (Aztec) ruler, a word meaning 'speaker'?
questions.explain: The ruler of Tenochtitlan was the huey tlatoani, or great speaker, chosen from a royal lineage by a council of nobles.

questions.q: In a Spanish colonial town, what was the cabildo?
questions.explain: Cabildos of leading citizens ran local affairs such as markets, streets and land grants under royal officials.

questions.q: In colonial New Spain and Peru, what was an obraje?
options: A silver mine owned by the crown
A mission school for Native children
A textile workshop often run with forced Native labor
questions.explain: Obrajes wove woolen and cotton cloth for colonial markets and were notorious for locking in debt-bound workers.

questions.q: Spain began settling which Caribbean island in 1509 and held it until England seized it in 1655?
questions.explain: Spanish Jamaica's first capital was Sevilla la Nueva on the north coast; England's capture came under Oliver Cromwell.

questions.q: Which Taino leader, who fled Hispaniola to organize resistance in Cuba, was burned at the stake by the Spanish around 1512?
questions.explain: Hatuey is remembered in Cuba as an early hero of resistance to colonial rule.

questions.q: The ball used in the Mesoamerican ballgame was a solid ball made from what?
questions.explain: Mesoamericans mixed latex with juice from morning glory vines to make bouncy rubber thousands of years before Europeans did.

questions.q: Casa Grande, a four-story building of caliche mud raised near the Gila River in present-day Arizona around 1350, was built by which people?
questions.explain: Openings in its walls line up with the sun and moon at key times, suggesting it served as an astronomical marker.

questions.q: Native peoples of the northern woodlands built light canoes covered with the bark of which tree?
questions.explain: Birchbark canoes were light enough to carry around rapids, which made them ideal for the river routes of the fur trade.

questions.q: The Wendat (Huron) of present-day southern Ontario traded surplus of which crop to Algonquian hunting peoples farther north?
questions.explain: In return the Wendat received furs, fish and meat, and their trade network later became central to the French fur trade.

questions.q: Kiliaen van Rensselaer, an Amsterdam merchant, held the most successful patroonship in New Netherland. Where was Rensselaerswyck?
options: On western Long Island near Brooklyn
Along the Delaware River near Philadelphia
Along the upper Hudson near present-day Albany
On Staten Island at the harbor mouth
questions.explain: Van Rensselaer never visited; his tenants farmed a vast estate whose manor lasted into the 1800s.

questions.q: New York's Brooklyn and Harlem take their names from what?
options: English lords who held land grants
questions.explain: Breuckelen and Nieuw Haarlem were named for Breukelen and Haarlem in the Dutch Republic.

questions.q: Edward Winslow's letter describing the 1621 harvest celebration at Plymouth, attended by the Wampanoag leader and about 90 of his men, was published in what 1622 pamphlet?
questions.explain: Winslow's letter and William Bradford's later history are the only firsthand accounts of the event.

questions.q: The Cambridge Platform of 1648 set out what system of church government for New England Puritans?
options: Rule by bishops appointed by the crown
Congregationalism, with each church governing itself
A single colony-wide synod that chose all ministers
Elected elders who answered to the Church of Scotland
questions.explain: The platform also declared that civil magistrates should punish heresy and protect the churches.

questions.q: Harvard College was named in 1639 for John Harvard, a young minister who did what?
options: Served as the college's first president
Wrote the colony's first law code
Left the college his library and half his estate
questions.explain: Harvard died of tuberculosis in 1638, leaving about 400 books and roughly 780 pounds.

questions.q: In 1665 Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck, a Wampanoag from Martha's Vineyard, became the first Native American to do what?
options: Be ordained as a Puritan minister
questions.explain: He studied at Harvard's Indian College, built in the 1650s, but died of tuberculosis within a year of graduating.

questions.q: New Haven Colony, founded in 1638 by John Davenport and Theophilus Eaton, stood out even among Puritan colonies for what?
options: Holding trials without juries, since the Bible did not mention them
Granting the vote to every adult man regardless of faith
Welcoming Quakers and Baptists as full citizens
Electing its governor by a vote of all church members, men and women
questions.explain: New Haven based its laws closely on scripture; it was absorbed into Connecticut under the 1662 charter.

questions.q: The Collegiate School, founded in Connecticut in 1701, was renamed in 1718 for which donor, a merchant who had grown rich in India?
questions.explain: Yale's gift of nine bales of goods, 417 books and a portrait of King George I helped pay for the college's first building in New Haven.

questions.q: Roger Williams's 1643 book A Key into the Language of America described what?
options: A plan to divide New England into towns
His theology of separating church and civil state
The language and customs of the Narragansett
The route from Boston to New Amsterdam
questions.explain: Williams wrote it on his voyage to England to get a charter for Providence Plantations.

questions.q: In 1679 the English crown separated which territory from Massachusetts and made it a royal province?
questions.explain: Massachusetts had governed the towns around Portsmouth since the 1640s; Maine stayed part of Massachusetts until 1820.

questions.q: In 1704 the 'Three Lower Counties' of Pennsylvania gained their own assembly, the start of which future state?
questions.explain: The counties of New Castle, Kent and Sussex shared Pennsylvania's governor until the Revolution.

questions.q: In 1702 East Jersey and West Jersey, which had been run separately by proprietors, were joined in what form?
questions.explain: Until 1738 the royal governor of New York also served as governor of New Jersey.

questions.q: Culpeper's Rebellion of 1677, in the Albemarle region of Carolina, grew out of anger at what?
options: A ban on settlement west of the mountains
The crown's plan to make Anglicanism the only faith
Collection of a Navigation Act duty on tobacco
Raids by Spanish forces from Florida
questions.explain: Rebels jailed the acting governor and customs collector and ran the colony for about two years.

questions.q: At the 1742 Battle of Bloody Marsh on St. Simons Island, James Oglethorpe's Georgia forces turned back an invasion launched from where?
questions.explain: The battle, part of the War of Jenkins' Ear, ended Spain's last serious attempt to take Georgia.

questions.q: Founded in Williamsburg in 1736 by printer William Parks, the Virginia Gazette was the first what in the colony?
questions.explain: It printed news, laws and advertisements, including notices offering rewards for people who had escaped slavery.

questions.q: Maryland's first colonists arrived in 1634 aboard which two ships?
options: The Susan Constant and the Discovery
questions.explain: More than a hundred settlers (estimates range from about 130 to 200), Catholic and Protestant, landed on St. Clement’s Island in March 1634.

questions.q: In 1695 Maryland moved its capital from its original settlement near the mouth of the Potomac to which town on the Severn River?
questions.explain: The move followed Protestant control of the colony after 1689; Annapolis was more central and had a fine harbor.

questions.q: Which Gulf Coast town served as the capital of French Louisiana from 1702 until 1720?
questions.explain: Bienville moved the settlement to its present site in 1711; the capital later shifted to Biloxi and then New Orleans.

questions.q: French farming villages of the Illinois Country, such as Kaskaskia, shipped what down the Mississippi to feed New Orleans?
questions.explain: Their open-field wheat farms, worked partly by enslaved people, made the Illinois Country a breadbasket for Louisiana.

questions.q: Spain built the Castillo de San Marcos at St. Augustine, begun in 1672, from coquina. What is coquina?
options: A volcanic rock shipped from Cuba
A soft limestone made of compacted shells
Clay bricks fired in local kilns
questions.explain: Coquina absorbed cannonballs instead of shattering, and the fort was never taken by force.

questions.q: Ville-Marie, founded in 1642 by Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve and Jeanne Mance as a Catholic mission, grew into which city?
questions.explain: Mance founded the settlement's hospital, the Hotel-Dieu; the island's location made it the hub of the fur trade.

questions.q: Acadian farmers around the Bay of Fundy turned tidal salt marshes into fields by building what?
options: Terraces cut into the coastal hillsides
Raised beds floating on rafts in the bay
Windmills that pumped water out to sea
Dikes with one-way sluice gates called aboiteaux
questions.explain: The gates let fresh water drain out at low tide but kept the sea from flowing in at high tide.

questions.q: In 1736 French forces under Bienville were defeated at Ackia, in present-day Mississippi, by which nation, trading partners of the English?
questions.explain: The Choctaw were France's allies in the war; the Chickasaw kept close ties with Carolina traders.

questions.q: In 1730 Sir Alexander Cuming took a delegation of which nation's leaders to London, where they signed a treaty of friendship and trade?
questions.explain: The seven visitors, including the young Attakullakulla, met King George II.

questions.q: The Westo, armed raiders who sold Native captives to Virginia and Carolina traders, were crushed in 1680 by whom?
options: The Spanish garrison at St. Augustine
Haudenosaunee war parties from New York
Carolina colonists and their Savannah allies
questions.explain: Carolina traders turned against the Westo to take over the Indian slave trade themselves.

questions.q: In the Great Swamp Fight of December 1675, colonial forces attacked a fortified winter town of which nation in Rhode Island?
questions.explain: Hundreds of Narragansett, many of them women and children, were killed, drawing the nation fully into King Philip's War.

questions.q: Ayuba Suleiman Diallo, a Muslim scholar from West Africa enslaved in Maryland in the 1730s, won his freedom after doing what?
options: Writing a letter in Arabic that reached England
Escaping to Spanish Florida by canoe
Suing his owner in a Maryland court
Buying himself with money from tobacco
questions.explain: Oglethorpe and others arranged his release; he returned home in 1734, and a memoir of his life was published in London.

questions.q: Lucy Terry Prince's poem 'Bars Fight,' about a 1746 raid near Deerfield, Massachusetts, is considered what?
options: The first poem printed in a colonial newspaper
The oldest known literary work by an African American
The first song written for a colonial militia
The earliest captivity narrative by a woman
questions.explain: Passed down orally for generations, it first appeared in print in 1854-55, in Josiah Holland’s Springfield newspaper and then his history of western Massachusetts.

questions.q: William Tennent's 'Log College' in Pennsylvania, begun around 1727, trained whom?
questions.explain: Its graduates, including Tennent's son Gilbert, became leaders of the Great Awakening; it is seen as a forerunner of Princeton.

questions.q: Kahal Kadosh Beth Elohim, a Jewish congregation organized in 1749, was founded in which colonial city?
questions.explain: By the late 1700s Charleston had one of the largest Jewish communities in North America.

questions.q: In early Massachusetts, wampum strings could legally be used for what until 1661?
questions.explain: Coins were scarce, so the colony accepted shell beads at set rates for small payments until it ended their legal-tender status.

questions.q: Michael Wigglesworth's 1662 poem The Day of Doom, a best seller in New England, described what?
questions.explain: Its long ballad stanzas warned sinners of damnation; many New England families owned a copy alongside the Bible.

questions.q: Sarah Kemble Knight's journal records her 1704-1705 journey on horseback from Boston to which city?
questions.explain: Her lively account of rough inns, river crossings and colonial manners was first published in 1825.

questions.q: Edward Randolph, sent to New England by the crown in 1676, reported that Massachusetts was doing what?
options: Secretly trading furs with the Spanish
Preparing to declare war on New France
Selling its charter to Dutch investors
Ignoring the Navigation Acts and royal authority
questions.explain: His reports helped lead to the 1684 cancellation of the Massachusetts charter.

questions.q: Which insect first reached Virginia in a shipment that arrived in 1622, an import that spread across North America ahead of settlers?
questions.explain: Honeybees are not native to the Americas; they were brought for honey and wax.

questions.q: William Bradford wrote of a 'mighty storm of wind and rain' that struck New England in August of which year?
questions.explain: The Great Colonial Hurricane of 1635 uprooted thousands of trees and wrecked ships along the coast.

questions.q: A powerful hurricane in September 1752 flooded which colonial port, driving ships into its streets?
questions.explain: The storm surge swept over the low-lying town, destroying wharves and many buildings.

questions.q: In 1630 the Massachusetts Bay Colony began paying bounties for killing which animal, a threat to colonists' livestock?
questions.explain: Bounties and clearing of forests had wiped out wolves from most of southern New England by the 1700s.

questions.q: In 1609 Samuel de Champlain joined Algonquin, Wendat and Montagnais allies in a battle against which nation, near the lake that now bears his name?
questions.explain: Champlain's guns killed several Mohawk leaders, starting decades of hostility between the Haudenosaunee and New France.

questions.q: To protect Mexico City from flooding, Spanish authorities began in 1607 a huge project to drain water from its lake basin. What was it called?
questions.explain: Enrico Martinez directed the work, which used Native laborers to dig a tunnel and later a great open cut at Huehuetoca.

questions.q: George Washington's great-grandfather John Washington came to Virginia in 1656 in what role?
options: As a minister of the Church of England
As a mate on a merchant ship trading for tobacco
As an indentured servant on a plantation
questions.explain: After the ship ran aground on the Potomac, he stayed, married and became a planter and militia officer.

questions.q: George Washington was born in 1732 at Popes Creek, on the Northern Neck peninsula, in which county?
questions.explain: The birthplace house burned in 1779; the site is now George Washington Birthplace National Monument.

questions.q: Washington spent much of his boyhood at Ferry Farm, across the Rappahannock River from which town?
questions.explain: His father Augustine died there in 1743, when George was eleven.

questions.q: In 1748 the sixteen-year-old George Washington joined a survey of western Virginia lands owned by which proprietor?
questions.explain: Fairfax's Northern Neck grant stretched to the Shenandoah Valley; the trip led to Washington's first job as a surveyor.

questions.q: In 1752 Lewis Hallam's company of London actors opened its first American season in which colonial capital?
questions.explain: They began with The Merchant of Venice; Puritan Boston still banned stage plays.

questions.q: In 1896 a hydroelectric plant at Niagara Falls began sending power to Buffalo, more than 20 miles away, using which system championed by George Westinghouse?
options: Direct current from Thomas Edison's dynamos
Compressed air piped through iron mains
Steam carried in insulated underground pipes
Alternating current based on Nikola Tesla's patents
questions.explain: The Adams Power Plant showed that alternating current could carry electricity long distances, settling the 'war of the currents.'

questions.q: Ottmar Mergenthaler's Linotype machine, first used by the New York Tribune in 1886, sped up what task?
options: Setting lines of type for printing
Sending news stories over telegraph lines
questions.explain: Casting a whole line of metal type at once let papers print more pages each day and helped make big-city dailies cheap.

questions.q: Frank W. Woolworth's chain of stores, which grew from a successful shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in 1879, was built on what idea?
options: Delivering goods ordered from a catalog by mail
Selling goods at fixed prices of five and ten cents
Letting customers buy goods on monthly credit
Selling only to members who paid a yearly fee
questions.explain: Woolworth's open counters and low fixed prices helped create the five-and-dime store.

questions.q: James B. Duke built his tobacco empire in the 1880s after adopting which invention, then formed the American Tobacco Company in 1890?
questions.explain: One Bonsack machine could roll as many cigarettes as dozens of hand workers; the Supreme Court broke up Duke's trust in 1911.

questions.q: Which soft drink did Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton create in 1886?
questions.explain: Pemberton sold it as a soda-fountain tonic; Asa Candler later bought the business and built it into a national brand.

questions.q: In 1891 a brawl in Valparaiso that killed two sailors from the USS Baltimore nearly led to war between the United States and which country?
questions.explain: Chile paid an indemnity of $75,000 after President Benjamin Harrison demanded an apology.

questions.q: An 1893 arbitration in Paris ruled against U.S. claims to control the Bering Sea in a dispute with Britain over hunting what?
questions.explain: The tribunal rejected U.S. claims but set hunting rules; the 1911 North Pacific Fur Seal Convention later saved the herds.

questions.q: In 1867, the same year as the Alaska purchase, the United States took possession of which uninhabited Pacific atoll?
questions.explain: Captain William Reynolds of the USS Lackawanna claimed it in August 1867; the Navy saw it as a possible coaling station.

questions.q: In 1873 Spanish authorities in Cuba executed dozens of crew and passengers, including Americans, from which captured ship, nearly causing war?
questions.explain: Secretary of State Hamilton Fish settled the crisis by diplomacy, and Spain later paid an indemnity.

questions.q: In November 1868 George Custer's 7th Cavalry attacked the Cheyenne camp of Black Kettle, who had survived Sand Creek, on which river in present-day Oklahoma?
questions.explain: Black Kettle and his wife were among those killed; the attack was part of Sheridan's winter campaign on the southern Plains.

questions.q: Congress admitted Utah as a state in 1896 only after Utah agreed to which condition, long demanded by federal officials?
options: Moving the capital from Salt Lake City
Giving up its public lands to railroads
questions.explain: The 1894 enabling act required the ban 'forever'; Utah's constitution also restored women's right to vote.

questions.q: In 1893, which state became the first where male voters approved women's suffrage in a popular referendum?
questions.explain: Wyoming had granted women the vote as a territory in 1869; Colorado's voters approved it by referendum in 1893.

questions.q: Johns Hopkins University, which opened in Baltimore in 1876, became a model for American universities by stressing what?
options: Free tuition for every student from Maryland
Military drill and engineering for officers
Manual labor as part of every course
Graduate study and research on the German model
questions.explain: Its graduate seminars, modeled on German universities, trained a generation of American scholars and set the pattern for the research university.

questions.q: Thomas Eakins's 1875 painting The Gross Clinic shocked many viewers with its frank depiction of what?
options: A surgery in progress before medical students
A lynching in a Southern town square
A strike by steelworkers in Pittsburgh
A bare-knuckle boxing match in a saloon
questions.explain: The Centennial Exhibition's art jury rejected it, and it hung instead in an Army hospital display at the fair.

questions.q: Hamlin Garland's 1891 story collection Main-Travelled Roads portrayed what?
options: High society in New York and Newport
The hard lives of Midwestern farm families
Mining camps of the California gold rush
questions.explain: Garland’s realism drew on his own youth on farms in Wisconsin and Iowa and his years in Dakota Territory.

questions.q: Which best-selling 1880 novel, subtitled A Tale of the Christ, was written by former Union general Lew Wallace?
questions.explain: Wallace finished it while serving as governor of New Mexico Territory; it became one of the best-selling American novels of the 1800s.

questions.q: Which Ohio-born poet won national fame with Lyrics of Lowly Life in 1896 and briefly worked at the Library of Congress?
questions.explain: Dunbar, whose parents had been enslaved in Kentucky, wrote in both standard English and dialect; he died in 1906.

questions.q: John Philip Sousa, born in Washington, D.C., led which band from 1880 to 1892 before writing 'The Stars and Stripes Forever'?
questions.explain: The Marine Band, 'The President's Own,' plays at the White House; Sousa's march became the national march by law in 1987.

questions.q: In 1869, which baseball club became the first to field a team of openly salaried professional players?
questions.explain: Managed by Harry Wright, the Red Stockings toured the country and went unbeaten in 1869.

questions.q: The bicycle craze of the 1890s, set off by the 'safety' bicycle with two equal wheels and a chain drive, had what social effect?
options: It ended the use of horses in American cities
It led Congress to build a national road network
It gave women more freedom to travel on their own
It made bicycles the main vehicle for mail delivery
questions.explain: Susan B. Anthony said in 1896 that the bicycle had done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.

questions.q: Which showman's touring Wild West exhibition, begun in 1883, featured sharpshooter Annie Oakley and, for one season, Sitting Bull?
questions.explain: Buffalo Bill's show turned the frontier into mass entertainment and toured Europe as well; Sitting Bull joined it in 1885.

questions.q: Engineer George Ferris built his giant observation wheel, more than 250 feet tall, for which event?
options: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago
The 1895 Cotton States Exposition in Atlanta
questions.explain: Chicago meant the wheel to outdo the Eiffel Tower, built for the 1889 Paris fair.

questions.q: In 1893, Clara Barton's American Red Cross spent months helping survivors of a hurricane that devastated which area?
options: The Sea Islands of South Carolina
The Outer Banks of North Carolina
questions.explain: The storm killed well over a thousand people, many of them Black farmers on islands near Beaufort.

questions.q: Beginning in 1871, the Fisk Jubilee Singers raised money for their Nashville university by doing what?
options: Selling a best-selling book of slave narratives
Holding a national lottery for Black schools
Touring the U.S. and Europe singing spirituals
questions.explain: They sang for President Grant in 1872 and for Queen Victoria in 1873, and their tours paid for Fisk's Jubilee Hall.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass served for more than twenty years as a trustee of which university in Washington, chartered by Congress in 1867?
questions.explain: Howard, named for Freedmen's Bureau commissioner Oliver O. Howard, admitted students regardless of race or sex.

questions.q: George Henry White of North Carolina, elected to the House in 1896, is remembered as what?
options: The last Black member of Congress for nearly 28 years
The first Black member to chair a House committee
The first Black Speaker of a state legislature
The only Black Democrat in Congress before 1935
questions.explain: When he left in 1901 he predicted Black Americans would return to Congress; Oscar De Priest was seated in 1929.

questions.q: Which Memphis-born educator living in Washington became the first president of the National Association of Colored Women in 1896?
questions.explain: Terrell, among the first Black women to earn a college degree, later helped win a 1953 case ending segregated restaurants in D.C.

questions.q: The Presidential Succession Act of 1886 placed whom next in line after the vice president?
options: The president pro tempore of the Senate
The Cabinet, starting with the secretary of state
The chief justice of the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Congress acted after Vice President Thomas Hendricks died in 1885; a 1947 law put the Speaker back in line.

questions.q: In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over bribes tied to what?
options: A trading post at a frontier Army fort
questions.explain: Belknap resigned just before the House voted; the Senate held a trial anyway, and he was acquitted.

questions.q: Chester Arthur hired which designer to redecorate the White House in 1882, adding a famous stained-glass screen to the entrance hall?
questions.explain: Arthur reportedly had wagonloads of old furnishings auctioned off; Theodore Roosevelt removed the Tiffany screen in 1902.

questions.q: First Lady Caroline Harrison served as the first president general of which organization founded in 1890?
options: The National American Woman Suffrage Association
The Daughters of the American Revolution
The General Federation of Women's Clubs
questions.explain: She also oversaw a major renovation of the White House and began its collection of presidential china.

questions.q: Francis Bellamy wrote the original Pledge of Allegiance in 1892 for school celebrations of what?
options: The 100th anniversary of the Bill of Rights
The 400th anniversary of Columbus's first voyage
questions.explain: It first appeared in the magazine The Youth's Companion, and schoolchildren recited it at Columbus Day events that October.

questions.q: Katharine Lee Bates wrote the poem 'America the Beautiful' after an 1893 trip to the summit of which mountain?
questions.explain: Bates, an English professor at Wellesley, first published the poem in 1895; it was later set to Samuel Ward's hymn tune.

questions.q: In 1876 a gang of counterfeiters tried to steal Abraham Lincoln's body from his tomb in Springfield, Illinois. What did they want?
options: A cash ransom and the release of a jailed engraver
Proof that Lincoln had not been murdered
Revenge for the hanging of the conspirators
The gold buttons buried with the president
questions.explain: Secret Service agents had been tipped off and broke up the plot; Lincoln's coffin was later sealed in concrete.

questions.q: In 1875, who had Mary Todd Lincoln declared insane at a court hearing in Chicago and committed to a private asylum?
questions.explain: She was released within months and declared sane by a court in 1876; she died in Springfield in 1882.

questions.q: John Wilkes Booth's brother Edwin, the leading Shakespearean actor of his day, founded what in New York in 1888?
options: The Players, a club for actors and artists
questions.explain: Edwin Booth gave his Gramercy Park house to the club and lived there until his death in 1893.

questions.q: In 1866 the American merchant ship General Sherman was burned and its crew killed after it sailed up the Taedong River toward which Korean city?
questions.explain: The incident fed American interest in forcing Korea, the 'Hermit Kingdom,' to open to trade.

questions.q: In 1871 a U.S. naval expedition stormed Korean forts on which island guarding the river approach to Seoul?
questions.explain: American forces won the fighting but withdrew without a treaty; Korea's government stayed closed to the U.S. for another decade.

questions.q: The 1882 treaty negotiated by Commodore Robert Shufeldt made the United States the first Western nation to do what?
questions.explain: The treaty with the Joseon kingdom promised 'good offices' if a third power treated either nation unjustly.

questions.q: Which ornate Second Empire building, finished in 1888 just west of the White House, housed three executive departments under one roof?
options: The State, War, and Navy Building
questions.explain: Designed by Alfred Mullett, it is now the Eisenhower Executive Office Building and holds White House staff offices.

questions.q: Congress created the National Zoological Park in Washington in 1889 partly at the urging of William Hornaday, who wanted to save which animal?
questions.explain: Hornaday kept bison on the Mall behind the Smithsonian Castle before the zoo opened; he later led the Bronx Zoo.

questions.q: Spencer Baird, later secretary of the Smithsonian, headed which federal agency created in 1871 to study declining fish stocks?
questions.explain: Baird set up a marine lab at Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and the commission raised and stocked fish across the country.

questions.q: Which federal agency, created in 1879 with Clarence King as its first director, mapped the nation's land and mineral resources?
questions.explain: John Wesley Powell succeeded King in 1881 and expanded the survey's mapping of the arid West.

questions.q: The 1894 Hinckley fire, which killed more than 400 people, raced through logged-over pine land in which state?
questions.explain: Slash left by loggers fueled the firestorm; trains carried hundreds of survivors to safety.

questions.q: In 1879 engineer James Eads completed jetties at the Mississippi River's South Pass. What were they meant to do?
options: Keep salt water out of New Orleans wells
Trap sediment to build new farmland
Make the river scour a deep channel for oceangoing ships
questions.explain: Narrowing the channel sped the current, which carried away silt and opened the port of New Orleans to large ships.

questions.q: Ferdinand de Lesseps, builder of the Suez Canal, led a French attempt to dig a canal across Panama in the 1880s. Why did it fail?
options: A U.S. naval blockade of the isthmus
A war between Colombia and France
questions.explain: Yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of workers, and the company collapsed in 1889 amid scandal.

questions.q: Sequoia National Park, created by Congress in 1890, was set aside mainly to protect what?
questions.explain: Congress created Yosemite National Park, also in California's Sierra Nevada, just days later.

questions.q: In the 1870s and 1880s, huge 'bonanza farms' using hired crews and machinery grew wheat in which region?
options: The Red River Valley of Dakota and Minnesota
questions.explain: Some covered tens of thousands of acres; many were set up by Northern Pacific Railroad investors.

questions.q: Audubon societies of the 1880s and 1890s, many led by women, campaigned against which fashion?
options: Hats decorated with wild bird feathers
questions.explain: Boston's Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall founded the Massachusetts Audubon Society in 1896 to fight the plume trade.

questions.q: From 1886 to 1918, who managed Yellowstone National Park?
questions.explain: Cavalry troops patrolled against poachers from Fort Yellowstone until the new National Park Service took over.

questions.q: In June 1898 the cruiser USS Charleston took which Pacific island from Spain, whose garrison had not heard that war had begun?
questions.explain: Spanish officers thought the American shots were a salute and rowed out to apologize for having no powder to return it.

questions.q: Which Librarian of Congress, serving from 1864 to 1897, pushed for the separate library building that opened across from the Capitol in 1897?
questions.explain: Spofford's push for copyright deposit swelled the collections until books were piled in the Capitol's halls.

questions.q: In 1875, which former president became the only one ever elected to the U.S. Senate after leaving the White House?
questions.explain: Tennessee's legislature elected him; he died a few months later. John Quincy Adams had served in the House after his presidency.

questions.q: When Grover Cleveland won in 1884, he became the first Democrat elected president since whom?
questions.explain: Republicans had held the White House for 24 years; Andrew Johnson had become president by succession, not election.

questions.q: In 1893, during a financial panic, Grover Cleveland secretly had surgery aboard a friend's yacht to remove what?
options: A bullet lodged near his spine
A tumor from the roof of his mouth
questions.explain: The operation was kept secret to avoid alarming markets; it was not confirmed publicly until 1917.

questions.q: On May 19, 1780, the sky over New England grew so dark at midday that people lit candles. What do researchers now think caused it?
options: Ash from a volcano in Iceland
A total eclipse of the sun
Smoke from huge wildfires in Canada
Dust blown from the Great Plains
questions.explain: A University of Missouri tree-ring study (published 2007, announced 2008) found fire scars in Ontario from 1780; smoke combined with fog and cloud to block the sun.

questions.q: During the winter of 1779-1780, among the harshest of the century, Washington's Continental Army camped near which New Jersey town?
questions.explain: Repeated blizzards buried the camp, and hungry soldiers suffered worse than they had at Valley Forge two years earlier.

questions.q: George Washington became president of the Patowmack Company in 1785. What was the company formed to do?
options: Make the Potomac navigable with canals around its falls
Survey the boundary of the new federal city
Run ferries between Virginia and Maryland
Drain the marshes along the Anacostia
questions.explain: Washington hoped the river would tie the western settlements to the East; the canal at Great Falls opened in 1802.

questions.q: In the 1790s George Washington built an unusual sixteen-sided barn at Mount Vernon. What was it designed for?
options: Drying tobacco leaves in the open air
Having horses tread wheat to separate the grain
Housing his herd of mules for the winter
Storing ice cut from the Potomac
questions.explain: Horses walked in circles on an upper floor of slatted boards, and the grain fell through to the floor below, out of the mud and weather.

questions.q: In 1784 Benjamin Franklin suggested that a dry fog over Europe and the harsh winter that followed might have been caused by what?
options: Smoke from coal fires in London
questions.explain: Iceland’s Laki fissure had erupted in 1783, releasing huge amounts of sulfur gases; Franklin, then in France, guessed at an Icelandic volcano (he named Hekla).

questions.q: In the 1820s a British fur company sent trapping brigades into the Snake River country to create a 'fur desert.' What was the goal?
options: Burn the grasslands to drive bison north into Canada
Settle farm families to block the Oregon Trail
Plant forts on every river leading to California
Trap out the beaver so Americans would have no reason to come
questions.explain: Hudson's Bay Company leader Peter Skene Ogden's brigades stripped the streams of beaver to keep American trappers out of the Oregon Country.

questions.q: During the War of 1812, enslaved miners dug large amounts of saltpeter from which Kentucky cave for making gunpowder?
questions.explain: The saltpeter works' wooden vats and pipes still survive in the cave, now a national park.

questions.q: In 1805 Lewis and Clark sent President Jefferson a live animal from Fort Mandan that survived the long trip east. What was it?
questions.explain: The expedition called it a 'barking squirrel'; a magpie from the same shipment also arrived alive.

questions.q: In the summer of 1805 Lewis and Clark spent about a month hauling their canoes and supplies around the Great Falls of which river?
questions.explain: The portage of about 18 miles, over prickly pear and rough ground, was one of the hardest stretches of the journey.

questions.q: In early 1863, Union troops tried to dig a canal across a bend in the Mississippi River. What did they hope to do?
options: Flood the Confederate capital at Richmond
Drain swamps to plant cotton for the Union
Link the river to Lake Pontchartrain
Bypass Vicksburg's guns on the bluffs
questions.explain: The canal across De Soto Point failed, and Grant instead marched his army south and crossed below the city.

questions.q: Nevada's Comstock Lode mines of the 1860s and 1870s used enormous amounts of timber to brace their tunnels. Where did much of it come from?
options: The redwood coast of northern California
questions.explain: Square-set timbering devoured whole forests in the Sierra Nevada, carried by flumes and railroads.

questions.q: California's Great Flood of 1862 was followed by a severe drought in 1863-1864. What was one result?
options: The founding of Los Angeles's water system
Huge cattle losses that broke many Californio ranchos
The end of the Gold Rush in the Sierra
A mass migration of farmers to Oregon
questions.explain: Hundreds of thousands of cattle died, and many Mexican-era ranch families lost land they had already been struggling to keep.

questions.q: The Lincoln Memorial, dedicated in 1922, stands on land that was what in the 1870s?
options: Tidal mudflats of the Potomac River
A plantation owned by the Custis family
questions.explain: Army engineers dredged the river channel from the 1880s and used the fill to create West Potomac Park.

questions.q: A fungus first identified at the Bronx Zoo in 1904 went on to kill billions of which tree, once common in eastern forests?
questions.explain: The blight, from imported Asian trees, wiped out mature chestnuts from Maine to Georgia within about 50 years.

questions.q: The hurricane of September 21, 1938, which struck with almost no warning and killed hundreds of people, devastated which region?
questions.explain: Storm surge swept away beach communities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, and winds felled millions of trees.

questions.q: Which mission's crew took the 1968 'Earthrise' photograph of the earth rising over the moon?
questions.explain: Bill Anders took the photo on December 24, 1968; it is often credited with inspiring the environmental movement.

questions.q: The first Landsat satellite, launched in 1972, was designed to do what?
options: Relay telephone calls across the Atlantic
Photograph the earth's land to track resources
Measure the ozone layer over Antarctica
questions.explain: Landsat images have recorded changes such as deforestation, farming and urban growth for decades.

questions.q: Launched in 1960, TIROS-1 was the first successful satellite of what kind?
questions.explain: In 78 days it sent back thousands of images of cloud cover, showing how satellites could track storms.

questions.q: Glen Canyon Dam on the Colorado River, whose gates closed in 1963, created which reservoir?
questions.explain: Environmentalists mourned the canyons it flooded; the Sierra Club had agreed to it in exchange for blocking the Echo Park dam.

questions.q: Redwood National Park, created by Congress in 1968, protects old-growth forest in which state?
questions.explain: Congress expanded the park in 1978 to protect streams from logging upslope of the tallest trees.

questions.q: Hurricane Agnes in June 1972 caused record floods in which state, especially along the Susquehanna River?
questions.explain: Agnes was a weak storm at landfall but dropped enormous rain; Wilkes-Barre and Harrisburg were badly flooded.

questions.q: What purpose did Thomas Jefferson's 1,000-foot terraced vegetable garden at Monticello serve?
options: A kitchen garden worked only by hired English gardeners
A model farm for the University of Virginia
A nursery for trees sent to the federal city
A testing ground for hundreds of plant varieties
questions.explain: Jefferson recorded his plantings in a Garden Book and grew vegetables from around the world, including seeds from the Lewis and Clark expedition.

questions.q: In 1774 Thomas Jefferson bought which Virginia landmark, later calling it 'the most sublime of Nature's works'?
questions.explain: Jefferson acquired the limestone arch and surrounding land from King George III's government and described it in Notes on the State of Virginia.
